title: Pendulum and resonance: pushing in time
objective: Learners see that a pendulum shaken by a small, steady push swings enormously when the push arrives at its natural frequency and barely at all when it does not, that damping sets how high and how sharp the peak is and how long the swing takes to build, and that the amplitude-against-frequency curve is the whole story in one picture.

recommended.why: The swing itself is the experience: p5 draws the shaken pivot, the bob and the growing arc in real time, so the ring-up is felt before it is read.

alternative.why: The animation shows one drive frequency at a time; the response curve shows every frequency at once with the current one marked. Which one teaches resonance, and which one proves it?

assumptions: Small-angle (linear) pendulum: the drive is weak, so the swing stays under about 35° and the closed-form response curve applies
The pivot is shaken sideways with a fixed small strength; the controls change the drive frequency as a ratio of the natural frequency, the damping ratio and the pendulum length
Natural frequency from the length (ω₀ = √(g/L), g = 9.81 m/s²); the swing is integrated with RK4 at 60 samples a second from rest
The steady-state amplitude is a / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) and the peak sits at r = √(1 − 2ζ²); the damping time constant is 1/(ζω₀)
Playback runs in real time for 24 s
units: angle: radians in the model, degrees on screen
frequency: ratio of drive to natural frequency; natural frequency in Hz from the length
checkDescription: The response curve peaks where the closed form says (r = √(1 − 2ζ²)); the steady amplitude at the chosen drive equals the curve there; the integrated swing agrees with it within 12 % once the transient has died; the series starts at rest and stays in the small-angle range.

learnerPrompts.predict: Set the drive to 1.6 × before you play. Will the swing be bigger or smaller than at 1.0 ×, and will it lag the push by more or less than 90°?
learnerPrompts.explain: Raise the damping to 0.5. The peak flattens and moves left. Explain what a service team gains and loses by adding "damping" (back-off, jitter) to retries.
